title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks, Runbooks and Known Issues
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This consolidated reference covers the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes for the current minor release, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki pointers. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and performance-focused ML engineers who operate and optimize inference in Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments.

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary:
- Service name: rwinf-runtime (internal).
- Purpose: low-latency, high-throughput transformer inference with quantization and KV cache support.
- Deployment modes: hosted (multi-tenant), dedicated (reserved GPU pools), private (VPC / on-prem).

Key components:
- Frontend router (rwinf-router): request validation, auth, tenant routing, metric tagging.
- Admission controller: enforces per-tenant concurrency, rate limits, and batching policy.
- Worker pool (rwinf-worker): GPU worker processes hosting compiled model binaries.
- Kernel selector (rwinf-kselector): chooses tuned CUDA/ROCm kernels at model load and dynamically adjusts per workload.
- KV-cache service (rwinf-kvcache): optional in-memory prefix cache with LRU eviction and TTL.
- Telemetry & tracing (rwinf-observability): token-level metrics aggregator, tracing hooks, and cost accounting.

SLOs and targets:
- P95 generation latency (short prompts, <=256 tokens): <= 120ms for gpt-small variants on p4d-like nodes.
- P50 generation latency: <= 40ms.
- Throughput goal (per-GPU): 40-120 concurrent low-latency streams depending on model and quantization.
- Availability SLA (Dedicated): 99.95% monthly.

Ownership:
- Runtime architecture: eng-serving-runtime core team.
- Kernel selector and profiling tools: perf-engineering subteam.
- Observability/instrumentation: eng-platform.

2) Kernel scheduling and selection

Design goals:
- Maximize utilization without violating latency SLOs.
- Prefer memory-efficient kernels for quantized models; prefer low-latency kernels for latency-critical routes.
- Allow fast runtime swapping of kernel variants per-model-version.

Scheduling concepts:
- Execution lanes: GPU resources are partitioned into logical "lanes" (latency, throughput, offload). Requests tagged with a priority (latency|best_effort) are mapped to lanes.
- Kernel profiles: each model+quantization combination ships with a profile: {preferred_kernel, max_batch, seq_threshold, memory_est}. Profiles are stored in catalog and can be overridden per-customer.
- Eviction and preemption: latency lane preempts throughput lane by soft-preempt (finish current micro-batch) and by token-level priority escalation.

Tuning knobs (config keys):
- kernel_selector.prefer_low_latency = true|false
- scheduler.max_batch_per_lane = int
- scheduler.per_route_concurrency = int
- kernel_selector.fallback_order = ["fp16_fast", "int8_memoptim", "fp32_stable"]

CLI: Inspect current kernel assignments
$ rwinfctl kernel list --model resnet-transformer-v1 --format json

Example profile (catalog JSON snippet):
{
  "model": "rwinf-gpt-medium",
  "quant": "int8",
  "preferred_kernel": "int8_qgemm_v4",
  "max_batch": "24",
  "seq_threshold": "1024",
  "notes": "Good for chat-like workloads where memory is limited"
}

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile a new model and iterate)

Step-by-step procedure:
1. Local compile and micro-benchmark
   - Build model binary with rwinf-compiler: rwinf-compiler --model model.pt --opt-level production --out /tmp/model.bin
   - Micro-bench kernels: rwinf-bench --binary /tmp/model.bin --batch 1,4,8 --seq 32,128,512 --metrics latency,throughput,memory --out /tmp/bench.json
2. Generate realistic traffic shape
   - Capture representative request traces from rwinf-observability (last 7 days). Use the trace-synth tool: trace-synth --input traces.ndjson --scale 1.
3. Full-node profiling (staging)
   - Deploy binary to staging worker pool with 1 replica: rwinfctl deploy --pool staging-perf --binary /tmp/model.bin --traffic 0%
   - Run perf harness: rwinf-perf-harness --workload /tmp/trace-synth.json --duration 30m --collect traces,profiles,device-stats --out /tmp/staging-profile.tar.gz
4. Analyze hot paths
   - Use profiling UI (http://perf.internal/rwinf) or run rwinf-analysis /tmp/staging-profile.tar.gz. Look for: kernel stalls, memory thrashing (OOM score), CUDA memcpy hotspots, and scheduler queueing.
5. Iterate: change compilation flags, kernel order, batching limits, or model quantization. Repeat micro-bench and full-node tests.

Profiling checklist:
- Confirm mem utilization per-GPU < 90% for steady-state.
- Verify p99 token latency within target.
- Confirm that KV-cache hit-rate (if enabled) is > 60% for conversational workloads.
- Validate fallback ordering under high load (simulate node drain).

4) Benchmarking suite (reference tests and metrics)

Bench categories:
- Microbench: per-kernel latency and memory (single-batch, single-GPU).
- Service bench: end-to-end API latency under admission + routing.
- Mixbench: mixed workload with streaming + embeddings + reranking.
- Regression bench: nightly suite comparing head vs baseline model/runtime commit.

Key metrics collected:
- Per-token latency percentiles (p50,p95,p99).
- Throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec).
- GPU utilization and SM occupancy.
- Memory high-water mark and allocator fragmentation.
- Scheduler queue depth and preempt events per minute.

Running the suite (example):
$ rwinf-ci run-bench --suite regression --baseline commit:abc123 --target HEAD --duration 2h --report s3://rwinf-perf/reports/2026-03-04.json

Interpreting results:
- Regression threshold: a change is flagged if p95 latency increases by >10% AND throughput drops >8% on at least two model variants.
- Quality gate: a minor slowdown that does not impact p99 or error rate may be allowed with opt-in rollout.

5) Release notes (current minor release: 2026.03.1)

Highlights:
- Kernel selector v2.4: introduction of dynamic kernel-stickiness heuristic (reduces kernel switch thrash by 35% on average).
- New int4 quant backend (experimental) with ~2x memory reduction for medium models; enabled behind opt-in flag.
- Scheduler improvements: soft-preempt for latency lane implemented; default per-route concurrency decreased from 12 to 8 to reduce queuing.
- Observability: token-level cost accounting added to trace exports.

Upgrade notes:
- Default scheduler.per_route_concurrency lowered; if you rely on higher concurrency for throughput, set per-route override: 
  scheduler.per_route_concurrency: 12
- int4 backend requires model re-compilation via rwinf-compiler --quant int4.

6) Known issues (active and tracked)

- Issue #RRT-4123: Intermittent OOMs on p4d-like machines when mixed fp16 + int8 kernels are loaded. Workaround: restart worker pool; set kernel_selector.fallback_order to prefer mem-optimized kernels. Owner: Marco Silva.
- Issue #RRT-4190: KV-cache replication lag under network partitions causing stale completions for private deployments. Workaround: reduce kvcache.replication_factor to 1 until fixed. Owner: Lena Rodriguez.
- Issue #RRT-4212: Small increase in p99 latency for streaming endpoints when soft-preempt triggers frequently. Mitigation: tune scheduler.max_batch_per_lane and increase lane count. Owner: Ravi Patel.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

Runbook: Latency spike (P95/P99 degradation)
1. Triage (5 min)
   - Dashboard: open rwinf-runtime > latency overview. Confirm which model, route, pool.
   - Check recent deploys: rwinfctl deploys --since 1h
2. Quick mitigations (10 min)
   - If new kernel or model version: rollback to previous model: rwinfctl rollback --model <model> --to-rev <rev>
   - Scale up latency lane: rwinfctl scale --pool <pool> --lane latency:+2
   - Apply temporary per-route concurrency reduction: rwinfctl config set --route <route> scheduler.per_route_concurrency=6
3. Deep analysis (30-60 min)
   - Collect perf bundle: rwinf-collect --pool <pool> --since 10m --out /tmp/incident-bundle.tar.gz
   - Upload to perf UI and share with perf-engineering on #rwinf-perf.
4. Post-incident
   - Run regression bench comparing head vs previous stable commit.
   - Update runbook with root cause and remediation steps.

Runbook: OOM on worker node
1. Immediate (2-5 min)
   - Mark node unschedulable: kubectl cordon <node> (private deployments: use internal admin console).
   - Drain or restart worker process: systemctl restart rwinf-worker || docker restart rwinf-worker
2. Investigation (15-30 min)
   - Check /var/log/rwinf/worker.log for OOM stack.
   - Confirm memory high-water marks from metrics: rwinf-metrics query 'gpu_memory_hwm{node="<node>"}' --last 1h
3. Mitigation
   - If caused by mixed kernels: set kernel_selector.fallback_order to mem-optimized and recycle worker.

9) Appendix: sample configs and commands

Sample scheduler config (YAML):

scheduler:
  default_lane: latency
  lanes:
    - name: latency
      max_batch: 8
      concurrency: 8
    - name: throughput
      max_batch: 64
      concurrency: 4
  per_route_concurrency: 8
  max_batch_per_lane: 128

Enable int4 (experimental) in rwinfctl:
$ rwinfctl config set --key runtime.experimental.int4_enabled true

Collect perf bundle for support:
$ rwinf-collect --pool <pool> --since 15m --include logs,profiles,metrics --out /tmp/bundle.tar.gz
